findings.evidence: This is simply how patron behavior works, and no library that has tried it has ever found otherwise.
findings.fix: Name the specific source supporting generalization beyond the pilot branches: a comparison of the five pilot branches against the other five on relevant characteristics, a cited study of fine elimination at other library systems, or consortium-wide data, or narrow the recommendation to the branches the pilot actually covers.
findings.location: ## Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide, second paragraph
findings.violation: This section exists to justify extending the 5-branch, 18-month pilot result to all ten consortium branches, but the only generalizing principle offered is asserted as self-evidently true. No study, standard, regulation, precedent, or documented body of practice is named; a target reader who does not already hold the belief that fine elimination works uniformly everywhere has nothing to test the systemwide extrapolation against beyond the pilot's own narrower five-branch scope.

findings.evidence: A skeptic on the board points to overdue fines as a source of materials-replacement funding, and argues that eliminating them systemwide will leave a shortfall the consortium has not planned for. The branch renovation project remains on schedule for completion next spring.
findings.fix: Replace the renovation-schedule sentence with an actual answer to the revenue concern: a replacement funding source, a projected shortfall estimate, or an argument for why fine revenue was never material to the materials-replacement budget.
findings.violation: The section raises the one foreseeable objection the recommendation's own grounds leave open, that fine revenue funds materials replacement, but its final sentence changes subject to an unrelated renovation-schedule update and never answers it. The objection is raised and then abandoned rather than addressed, which this skill's operational test treats the same as never raising it.

findings.evidence: This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date; items still unreturned past that window remain subject to the existing replacement-cost billing process, matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established.
findings.fix: Report the pilot's windowed return-time data that supports the 60-day cutoff, or drop the claim that the window matches the pilot's pattern and justify the 60-day figure on its own terms, such as operational or replacement-cost-timing grounds.
findings.violation: The clause claims the 60-day window 'matches' a pattern the pilot data established, but the pilot section ("What the Pilot Showed") reports only an aggregate on-time-or-eventual return rate (93 percent versus 86 percent); no day-windowed return distribution appears anywhere in the artifact, so a reader has no stated evidence against which to check the claimed match.
